title: Trigonometric Equations
learningObjective: Find all solutions to a given trigonometric equation.

faqs.question: What's the difference between solving a trig equation "on an interval" versus finding the "general solution"?
faqs.answer: Solving on an interval, like \( [0, 2\pi) \), means listing only the solutions that fall in that one window. The general solution means describing every solution there is, on the entire number line in both directions, using a formula with an integer \( n \) — because sine, cosine, and tangent repeat forever, a trig equation almost always has infinitely many solutions.

faqs.question: Why does adding 2πn to a solution give another solution?
faqs.answer:
Adding \( 2\pi \) is exactly one full trip around the unit circle, which lands you back on the exact same point — same coordinates, same sine and cosine. So if \( \theta \) is a solution, \( \theta + 2\pi \), \( \theta - 2\pi \), \( \theta + 4\pi \), and so on all share that same point and are solutions too. Writing \( +2\pi n \) for any integer \( n \) captures all of them in one formula.

π/6, π/6 + 2π, π/6 − 2π, π/6 + 4π … all land on the exact same ray, so they all solve the equation. The general solution θ = π/6 + 2πn captures every one of them at once.

faqs.question: Why do I get ± when I take the square root of a squared trig term?
faqs.answer: This is the same square root property from algebra: if \( x^2 = k \), then \( x = \pm\sqrt{k} \), because both a positive and a negative number square to the same result. It's not optional — dropping the \( \pm \) throws away half of the true solutions, usually an entire quadrant's worth of angles.

faqs.question: Why might one factor of a factored trig equation have no solution?
faqs.answer:
Sine and cosine can only ever output a number from −1 to 1 — that's their range. If solving one factor requires sine or cosine to equal something outside that range, like 3, there's simply no angle that does that, so that branch contributes nothing to the final answer.

Sine and cosine only ever output values from −1 to 1 (axis broken here to fit "3" on the page). If solving one factor asks for a value outside that range, like cos θ = 3, that factor contributes nothing — it isn't a mistake, just an empty branch.

faqs.question: Why does an equation like sin(2θ) have more solutions on [0, 2π) than sin θ does?
How do I solve a basic trig equation like 2sinθ − 1 = 0 on an interval?
faqs.answer:
Use ordinary algebra to isolate the trig function on one side, just as you would isolate \( x \) in a linear equation. Then use the unit circle or reference angles (TR5) to find every angle in the interval with that value.
Worked Example — solve \( 2\sin\theta - 1 = 0 \) on \( [0, 2\pi) \)

\( 2\sin\theta = 1 \)  (add 1 to both sides)

\( \sin\theta = \dfrac{1}{2} \)  (divide by 2)

\( \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6}, \dfrac{5\pi}{6} \)  (the two Quadrant I/II angles with sine \( \tfrac{1}{2} \))

faqs.question: How do I write the general solution once I have the interval solutions?
faqs.answer:
Add \( +2\pi n \) (with \( n \) any integer) to each solution you found on \( [0, 2\pi) \). Each interval solution becomes its own family, since coterminal angles repeat every \( 2\pi \).
Worked Example — general solution of \( 2\sin\theta - 1 = 0 \)

Interval solutions: \( \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6}, \dfrac{5\pi}{6} \)

General solution: \( \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6} + 2\pi n \)  and  \( \theta = \dfrac{5\pi}{6} + 2\pi n, \; n \in \mathbb{Z} \)

faqs.question: How do I solve a trig equation that's already factored into two pieces (Zero Product Property)?
faqs.answer:
Set each factor equal to zero and solve the two simpler equations separately, exactly as you would for a factored polynomial equation. Combine every solution from both factors into one list at the end.
Worked Example — solve \( (2\sin\theta+\sqrt{3})(\cos\theta-1) = 0 \) on \( [0, 2\pi) \)

\( 2\sin\theta+\sqrt{3}=0 \Rightarrow \sin\theta=-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \Rightarrow \theta=\dfrac{4\pi}{3},\dfrac{5\pi}{3} \)

\( \cos\theta-1=0 \Rightarrow \cos\theta=1 \Rightarrow \theta=0 \)

All solutions: \( \theta = 0, \dfrac{4\pi}{3}, \dfrac{5\pi}{3} \)

faqs.question: How do I solve an equation like 4 = 5 + tan θ that involves a different trig function?
faqs.answer:
The algebra step is identical no matter which trig function is involved — isolate it first. What changes is the last step: use the reference angles and quadrant signs for that specific function (tangent's period is π, not 2π, so watch for that when you write the general solution).
Worked Example — solve \( 4 = 5+\tan\theta \) on \( [0, 2\pi) \)

\( \tan\theta = -1 \)  (subtract 5 from both sides)

\( \theta = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}, \dfrac{7\pi}{4} \)  (tangent is \( -1 \) in Quadrants II and IV)

General solution: \( \theta = \dfrac{3\pi}{4} + 2\pi n \) and \( \theta = \dfrac{7\pi}{4} + 2\pi n \)

faqs.question: How do I use the square root property on an equation like 4sin²θ − 2 = 0?
faqs.answer:
Isolate the squared trig function first, then take the square root of both sides, keeping both the positive and negative case.
Worked Example — solve \( 4\sin^2\theta - 2 = 0 \) on \( [0, 2\pi) \)

\( \sin^2\theta = \dfrac{1}{2} \)  (isolate)

\( \sin\theta = \pm\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{2}} = \pm\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \)  (square root property, then rationalize — see faq-11)

\( \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{4}, \dfrac{3\pi}{4}, \dfrac{5\pi}{4}, \dfrac{7\pi}{4} \)  (all four quadrants, since both signs are needed)

faqs.question: How do I know which form of a square root value to use (√(1/2) vs √2/2)?
faqs.answer: They're the same number, just written differently — \( \sqrt{\tfrac{1}{2}} \) rationalizes to \( \tfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \). Use whichever form you actually recognize on the unit circle (TR5); \( \tfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \) is the standard form that appears there, so it's usually the more useful one to convert to.

faqs.question: How do I factor out a GCF from a trig equation like 2sinθcosθ − √2cosθ = 0?
faqs.answer:
Look for a factor common to every term — here it's cos θ — pull it out front, and apply the Zero Product Property to the result. Never divide both sides by a trig expression to cancel it, since that can quietly delete an entire family of solutions; factoring keeps every solution intact.
Worked Example — solve \( 2\sin\theta\cos\theta - \sqrt{2}\cos\theta = 0 \) on \( [0, 2\pi) \)

\( \cos\theta(2\sin\theta - \sqrt{2}) = 0 \)  (factor out the GCF, \( \cos\theta \))

\( \cos\theta = 0 \Rightarrow \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{3\pi}{2} \)

\( 2\sin\theta-\sqrt{2}=0 \Rightarrow \sin\theta=\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \Rightarrow \theta=\dfrac{\pi}{4}, \dfrac{3\pi}{4} \)

All solutions: \( \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{4}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{3\pi}{4}, \dfrac{3\pi}{2} \)

faqs.question: How do I solve a "quadratic in form" trig equation like 2cos²θ − 5cosθ − 3 = 0?
faqs.answer:
Mentally replace the trig function with \( x \), factor the resulting quadratic exactly as in algebra, then switch back and apply the Zero Product Property.
Worked Example — solve \( 2\cos^2\theta - 5\cos\theta - 3 = 0 \) on \( [0, 2\pi) \)

Let \( x=\cos\theta \): \( 2x^2-5x-3 = (2x+1)(x-3) \)

So \( (2\cos\theta+1)(\cos\theta-3)=0 \)

\( 2\cos\theta+1=0 \Rightarrow \cos\theta=-\dfrac{1}{2} \Rightarrow \theta=\dfrac{2\pi}{3},\dfrac{4\pi}{3} \)

\( \cos\theta-3=0 \Rightarrow \cos\theta=3 \) — no solution (faq-14)

faqs.question: What do I do when a factor from a quadratic-form equation gives no valid solution?
faqs.answer:
Simply drop that branch and report only the solutions from the factor that actually works. This is normal and expected — the algebra of factoring doesn't know sine and cosine are limited to [−1, 1], so it can produce a factor that asks for an impossible value. It isn't a mistake in your work; it's just an empty branch.
Worked Example

From faq-13: \( \cos\theta=3 \) is impossible, so it's discarded.

Final answer: \( \theta = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}, \dfrac{4\pi}{3} \) only.

faqs.question: How do I solve an equation with a multiple angle like sin(2θ) = 1/2 for the general solution?
faqs.answer:
Temporarily replace the multiple angle with a single variable, like \( \alpha = 2\theta \), solve for \( \alpha \) as usual (interval solutions, then general solution), and only then substitute \( 2\theta \) back in and solve for \( \theta \) — dividing the whole general solution, period and all, by 2.
Worked Example — general solution of \( \sin(2\theta) = \dfrac{1}{2} \)

Let \( \alpha = 2\theta \): \( \sin\alpha = \dfrac{1}{2} \Rightarrow \alpha = \dfrac{\pi}{6}+2\pi n \) and \( \alpha = \dfrac{5\pi}{6}+2\pi n \)

Substitute back: \( 2\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6}+2\pi n \) and \( 2\theta = \dfrac{5\pi}{6}+2\pi n \)

Divide everything by 2: \( \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{12}+\pi n \) and \( \theta = \dfrac{5\pi}{12}+\pi n \)

Notice the period is now \( \pi \), not \( 2\pi \) — that's exactly what doubles the count of solutions (faq-5).

faqs.question: How do I find all solutions on [0, 2π) once I have the general solution for a multiple-angle equation?
faqs.answer:
Substitute \( n = 0, 1, 2, \ldots \) and then \( n = -1, -2, \ldots \) into each general-solution formula, keeping every result that lands inside \( [0, 2\pi) \). Stop in each direction as soon as a value falls outside the interval.
Worked Example — solutions of \( \sin(2\theta)=\dfrac{1}{2} \) on \( [0, 2\pi) \)

From \( \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{12}+\pi n \): \( n=0 \to \dfrac{\pi}{12} \); \( n=1 \to \dfrac{13\pi}{12} \); \( n=2 \to \dfrac{25\pi}{12} \) — too big, stop.

From \( \theta = \dfrac{5\pi}{12}+\pi n \): \( n=0 \to \dfrac{5\pi}{12} \); \( n=1 \to \dfrac{17\pi}{12} \); \( n=2 \) — too big, stop.

All four solutions: \( \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{12}, \dfrac{5\pi}{12}, \dfrac{13\pi}{12}, \dfrac{17\pi}{12} \)

faqs.question: How does solving these equations use everything from TR5, TE1, and TE2?
faqs.answer:
TR5's reference angles and quadrant signs are how you turn "sin θ = 1/2" into actual angle values, every single time. TE1's identities let you rewrite an equation into a solvable shape, most obviously in the multiple-angle and identity-substitution problems. TE2's habits of manipulating trig expressions — factoring, common denominators, rewriting in sine and cosine — are exactly the algebra skills this section runs on, just now used to solve for θ instead of to prove two sides equal.

A quick chooser for where to start. More than one row can apply to the same equation — work through them in order.

faqs.question: Why does solving trigonometric equations matter beyond this course?
faqs.answer: Any process that repeats — a wave, a season, a rotating machine part, an alternating current — is described by a trig function, and answering "when does this reach a certain value?" means solving a trig equation. This shows up directly in physics (oscillation and waves), engineering (signal processing, AC circuits), and it's also the exact skill needed in calculus whenever a problem asks where a periodic function crosses zero or hits a maximum.

guided.title: Practice Isolating and Solving on an Interval
guided.prompt: I'm learning to solve basic trig equations. Give me an equation like 2sinθ − 1 = 0 or 4 = 5 + tanθ, and walk me through isolating the trig function with algebra, then finding every solution on [0, 2π) using reference angles. Give me a few more of increasing difficulty and check my work.

guided.title: Practice Writing General Solutions
guided.prompt: I'm learning to write the general solution of a trig equation. Give me a few equations, have me find the solutions on [0, 2π) first, and then coach me through writing the +2πn general solution for each. Include at least one tangent equation, where the period is different.

guided.title: Practice Factoring Trig Equations
guided.prompt: Give me trig equations that need the Zero Product Property, GCF factoring, or quadratic-in-form factoring (letting x = cos θ or similar). Walk me through identifying which kind it is, factoring it, and solving each resulting piece. Include one equation where a factor gives no valid solution, and ask me to explain why.

guided.title: Practice the Square Root Property
guided.prompt: I'm learning to solve equations with a squared trig function, like 4sin²θ − 2 = 0. Walk me through isolating the squared term, applying the square root property with both signs, and finding every solution across all four quadrants. Check that I don't drop the negative case.

guided.title: Practice Multiple-Angle Equations
guided.prompt: I'm learning to solve equations like sin(2θ) = 1/2. Walk me through substituting α for the multiple angle, solving for α's general solution, substituting back, and dividing to solve for θ. Then have me plug in n = 0, 1, 2, −1 to find every solution on [0, 2π), and check that I stop at the right point in each direction.

stages.desc: Three quick reviews TE3 leans on: the unit circle in reverse (TR5), tangent and reciprocal functions, and the algebra of isolating and square roots. Skip any you already have.

stops.title: Unit circle in reverse
stops.target: Given a sine or cosine value, find every angle in \([0,2\pi)\) with that value (TR5). Sine is a height (horizontal line); cosine is a width (vertical line).
stops.coldPlain: Find all theta in [0, 2pi): (1) cos theta = -1/2 (2) sin theta = sqrt3/2
stops.solution: (1) Reference angle pi/3; cosine negative in Quadrants II and III: 2pi/3 and 4pi/3. (2) Reference angle pi/3; sine positive in Quadrants I and II: pi/3 and 2pi/3.
stops.mistake: Stopping at one angle; most values appear twice in [0, 2pi).
stops.reflect: Why does a horizontal line usually hit the unit circle twice?

stops.title: Tangent and the reciprocal functions
stops.target: Find angles for \(\tan\theta\), and turn \(\csc\), \(\sec\), \(\cot\) equations into \(\sin\), \(\cos\), \(\tan\) by flipping.
stops.coldPlain: Find all theta in [0, 2pi): (1) tan theta = -1 (2) csc theta = 2
stops.solution: (1) Tangent is -1 where sin and cos are opposites: Quadrants II and IV, 3pi/4 and 7pi/4. (2) csc theta = 2 means sin theta = 1/2: pi/6 and 5pi/6.
stops.mistake: Treating csc theta = 2 as sin theta = 2 (no solution) instead of flipping to 1/2.
stops.reflect: Why are tangent solutions always exactly pi apart?

stops.title: Algebra: isolate, square roots, rationalize
stops.target: Solve linear and squared equations for \(x\), keep both signs of a square root, and rationalize (\(\sqrt{\tfrac12}=\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\)).
stops.solution: (1) 2x = sqrt3, x = sqrt3/2. (2) x^2 = 3/4, x = plus or minus sqrt3/2. (3) x^2 = 1/2, x = plus or minus 1/sqrt2 = plus or minus sqrt2/2.
stops.mistake: Writing only the positive square root.
stops.reflect: Every TE3 equation is one of these with sin, cos, or tan in place of x. Which algebra step is slowest for you?

stages.desc: Isolate and solve on [0, 2π), all solutions with 2πk, reciprocal functions, squared functions, multiple angles, and factoring.

stops.title: Isolate, then use the unit circle
stops.target: Solve on \([0,2\pi)\): isolate the trig function with algebra, find the reference angle, then pick the quadrants from the sign.
stops.note: Show the isolated trig function, the reference angle, which quadrants you used and why, and whether the question asks for [0, 2pi) or all solutions.
stops.solution: sin theta = -sqrt2/2. Reference angle pi/4. Sine is negative in Quadrants III and IV: 5pi/4 and 7pi/4.
stops.mistake: Answering -pi/4, which is not in [0, 2pi); its coterminal angle 7pi/4 is.
stops.reflect: How does the sign of the value tell you which quadrants to use?

stops.title: All solutions: add 2πk
stops.target: "Find all solutions" means every angle, not just \([0,2\pi)\). Find the solutions in \([0,2\pi)\), then add \(2\pi k\) to each.
stops.coldPlain: Find all solutions of 2 cos theta - sqrt3 = 0.
stops.note: Show the isolated trig function, the reference angle, which quadrants you used and why, and whether the question asks for [0, 2pi) or all solutions.
stops.solution: cos theta = sqrt3/2 gives pi/6 and 11pi/6 in [0, 2pi). Cosine repeats every 2pi, so all solutions are pi/6 + 2pi k and 11pi/6 + 2pi k for every integer k.
stops.mistake: Writing only pi/6 + 2pi k and losing the second family.
stops.againA: \(\tan\theta=\tfrac{\sqrt3}{3}\): \(\theta=\tfrac{\pi}{6}+2\pi k,\ \tfrac{7\pi}{6}+2\pi k\) (the same angles as \(\tfrac{\pi}{6}+\pi k\)).
stops.reflect: Look at the graph: what does k count?

stops.title: Equations with csc, sec, or cot
stops.target: Isolate the reciprocal function, flip to sine, cosine, or tangent, and simplify the value before you use the unit circle.
stops.coldPlain: Find all solutions of 3 csc theta - 2 sqrt3 = 0.
stops.note: Show the isolated trig function, the reference angle, which quadrants you used and why, and whether the question asks for [0, 2pi) or all solutions.
stops.solution: csc theta = 2sqrt3/3. Flip: sin theta = 3/(2sqrt3) = sqrt3/2. That gives pi/3 and 2pi/3, so pi/3 + 2pi k and 2pi/3 + 2pi k.
stops.mistake: Flipping 2sqrt3/3 to 3/(2sqrt3) and not recognizing it as sqrt3/2 (multiply top and bottom by sqrt3).
stops.reflect: Why is it safer to flip to sin, cos, or tan than to memorize csc, sec, cot values?

stops.title: Squared trig functions: ± gives four angles
stops.target: Isolate \(\sin^2\theta\) or \(\cos^2\theta\), take both square roots, and solve each sign separately.
stops.note: Show the isolated trig function, the reference angle, which quadrants you used and why, and whether the question asks for [0, 2pi) or all solutions.
stops.solution: cos^2 theta = 3/4, so cos theta = plus or minus sqrt3/2. Positive: pi/6, 11pi/6. Negative: 5pi/6, 7pi/6. Four solutions.
stops.mistake: Taking only cos theta = sqrt3/2 and stopping at two answers.
stops.stretch: Solve \(\sin^2\theta-1=0\) on \([0,2\pi)\). Why are there only two answers?
stops.stretchA: \(\sin\theta=\pm1\): \(\theta=\tfrac{\pi}{2},\tfrac{3\pi}{2}\). The lines \(y=1\) and \(y=-1\) only touch the circle once each.
stops.reflect: Look at the picture: how do the two vertical lines explain why there are four answers?

stops.title: Multiple angles: sin(3θ), cos(2θ)
stops.target: For \(\sin(c\theta)\) on \([0,2\pi)\), let \(\alpha=c\theta\). Then \(\alpha\) runs over \([0,2c\pi)\): find every \(\alpha\) there, then divide each by \(c\).
stops.note: Show the isolated trig function, the reference angle, which quadrants you used and why, and whether the question asks for [0, 2pi) or all solutions.
stops.solution: sin(3 theta) = 1/2. Let alpha = 3 theta; alpha goes from 0 to 6pi (three trips around the circle). alpha = pi/6, 5pi/6, 13pi/6, 17pi/6, 25pi/6, 29pi/6. Divide by 3: pi/18, 5pi/18, 13pi/18, 17pi/18, 25pi/18, 29pi/18.
stops.mistake: Solving sin alpha = 1/2 only in [0, 2pi), dividing by 3, and reporting just pi/18 and 5pi/18.
stops.reflect: Before solving, how can you predict how many answers sin(c theta) = k will have on [0, 2pi)?

stops.title: Factoring: quadratic form
stops.target: Treat the trig function like a variable, factor, set each factor to zero, and drop any factor that asks for an impossible value.
stops.coldPlain: Solve 2 sin^2 theta - sin theta - 1 = 0 on [0, 2pi).
stops.note: Show the isolated trig function, the reference angle, which quadrants you used and why, and whether the question asks for [0, 2pi) or all solutions.
stops.solution: Let u = sin theta: 2u^2 - u - 1 = (2u + 1)(u - 1). sin theta = -1/2 gives 7pi/6 and 11pi/6; sin theta = 1 gives pi/2.
stops.mistake: Dividing both sides by sin theta, which loses solutions.
stops.reflect: What would you do if one factor gave cos theta = 3?

stops.coldPlain: (1) Find all solutions of tan theta + 1 = 0. (2) Find all solutions in [0, 2pi) of 4 sin^2 theta - 1 = 0. (3) Find all solutions in [0, 2pi) of 2 cos(3 theta) + 1 = 0.
stops.note: Show the isolated trig function, the reference angle, which quadrants you used and why, and whether the question asks for [0, 2pi) or all solutions.
stops.solution: (1) tan theta = -1: 3pi/4 and 7pi/4 in [0, 2pi), so 3pi/4 + 2pi k and 7pi/4 + 2pi k. (2) sin^2 theta = 1/4, sin theta = plus or minus 1/2: pi/6, 5pi/6, 7pi/6, 11pi/6. (3) cos(3 theta) = -1/2; alpha = 3 theta in [0, 6pi): 2pi/3, 4pi/3, 8pi/3, 10pi/3, 14pi/3, 16pi/3; divide by 3.
stops.mistake: In (3), dividing 2pi/3 by 3 but forgetting the other trips around the circle.
stops.again: (1) Find all solutions of \(\csc\theta+2=0\). (2) Solve \(4\cos^2\theta-1=0\) on \([0,2\pi)\). (3) Solve \(2\sin(2\theta)-\sqrt3=0\) on \([0,2\pi)\).
stops.reflect: Which question type is trickiest: all solutions, squared, or multiple angle?
